newsitem.title: USA: U.S. says Iran remains premier "terrorism" sponsor.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says Iran remains premier "terrorism" sponsor.

text.p: The U.S. State Department said on Wednesday that Iran remained the chief sponsor of "international terrorism" in 1996, a year in which deaths from what it described as terror attacks nearly doubled.

In its annual report "Patterns of Global Terrorism," the department listed six other countries that it alleged also sponsored terrorism: Cuba, Iraq, Libya, North Korea, Sudan and Syria. All seven have been on the past three annual lists.

The report said that in 1996 Iran was "involved in the planning and execution of terrorist acts by its own agents and others such as the Lebanese Hizbollah and continued to fund and train known terrorist groups."
Philip Wilcox, the State Department's coordinator for what it terms counter-terrorism, said such attackers were aided by advances in weapons technology.

"Terrorists have increasing access to materials of mass destruction -- nuclear, chemical and biological," Wilcox said at a briefing. "And today's volatile mix of religious fanaticism, pathological terrorists, and other dangerous and perverse forces, and their access to modern technology increases the danger of terrorism tremendously."
Deaths from "international terrorism" acts nearly doubled to 311 in 1996 from 163 in 1995, the report said.
Wilcox said Iran had been responsible for more than 50 murders of dissidents overseas since 1990, and at least eight overseas murders in 1996.
On Tuesday, the United States applauded a decision by foreign ministers of the European Union to suspend ministerial ties with Iran.

State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said Washington shared the EU's view "that Iran must respect the norms of international law, refrain from acts of terrorism and live up to international commitments on human rights and on proliferation issues."

Specific cases of terrorism listed in the report's introduction were the truck bombing at the Al Khobar apartment complex in Saudi Arabia in which 19 U.S. airmen were killed, a series of suicide bombings in Israel that killed more than 60 people and the recent hostage-taking in Lima, Peru, by Marxist rebels.
The deadliest attack of 1996 was in Sri Lanka on January 31, when Tamil separatists killed 90 people with a truck bomb in central Colombo, the report said.

Also listed as a "significant attack" was a bomb detonated in a parking garage in London that killed two people and wounded more than 100 others. The Irish Republican Army claimed responsibility for that attack, the report said.

Appearance on the terrorism list triggers four sets of U.S. government sanctions. They include a ban on military sales and aid, controls over export of so-called "dual-use" items -- those items that can be used for either military or civilian purposes -- prohibitions on economic aid and imposition of miscellaneous financial and other sanctions.
The report said domestic terrorism in countries including Algeria, India, Sri Lanka and Pakistan appeared to be increasing "and is more serious, in gross terms, than international terrorism."

The State Department defined "terrorism" as "pre-meditated, politically motivated violence perpetrated against noncombatant targets by subnational groups or clandestine agents, usually intended to influence an audience."

Overall, there were 296 acts of international terrorism in 1996, the lowest annual total in 24 years and 144 fewer than in 1995, according to the report. But the toll of deaths and injuries was one of the highest on record: 311 killed and 2,652 wounded.
